*Disclosure: since this is an older project and I want to move forward, this blog post was generated by AI using my original report and documentation of the project.*

**TL;DR:** Follow-up to my [BVH/Grid comparison project](/projects/bvh-grid-raytracer) - this time I took BVH construction itself and made it fully parallel on the GPU using OpenCL, implementing Karras's LBVH (Linear BVH) algorithm from scratch: Morton codes, a GPU radix sort, parallel hierarchy construction, and bottom-up bounding box propagation. Then I benchmarked it against CPU LBVH and my old naive BVH across models ranging from 5K to 28 *million* triangles. GPU version wins big once scenes get large - up to 4.65x faster construction - at the cost of a barely-there hit to tree quality.

**Tech:** C++17, OpenCL 1.2, CMake

## The Goal

My previous BVH was built recursively on the CPU: pick an axis, split, recurse, repeat. That's fine for static scenes you build once and render many times. It falls apart the moment you need to rebuild the tree every frame - for animated meshes, deforming geometry, anything dynamic. Construction time stops being a footnote and becomes the bottleneck.

LBVH exists to fix exactly this. Instead of recursively partitioning space, you turn BVH construction into a sorting problem: assign every primitive a Morton code (a value that encodes its 3D position while preserving spatial locality), sort those codes, and the sorted order directly gives you a tree. Sorting parallelizes beautifully. Recursive spatial splitting does not. So the natural next question was: can I actually get this running on the GPU myself, end to end?

*Note: built on top of Peter Shirley's Ray Tracing: The Next Week (CC0 public domain base code), following Karras (2012) and Lauterbach et al. (2009). Benchmarked on an AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT at 1280x720, 100 samples/pixel (~92M rays per scene).*

## The Journey

#### The LBVH Pipeline

The whole thing came together as four GPU kernels:

- **Morton code computation:** each primitive's bounding-box centroid gets quantized onto a 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰ lattice and interleaved into a 30-bit Morton code - one GPU thread per primitive, trivially parallel.
- **Radix sort:** a full LSB-first parallel radix sort over the Morton codes, 4 bits per pass (8 passes total), built from three sub-kernels - per-block histogram construction, a Blelloch prefix scan over the histogram, and a scatter pass that writes primitives to their sorted positions.
- **Hierarchy construction:** Karras's single-kernel-launch tree build. One thread per internal node, each independently figuring out the range of leaves it covers via a binary search over Morton code common-prefix length, then locating its split point - no multi-pass tree building required.
- **Bounding box propagation:** a bottom-up pass where each leaf thread walks up through parent pointers, using atomic counters so that whichever thread arrives *second* at a node is the one that computes its bounding box - guaranteeing each node's AABB is computed exactly once with no race conditions.

I also added triangle primitives with Möller-Trumbore intersection and OBJ loading via tinyobjloader, since the previous project only really needed basic shapes. Then I built out a benchmarking harness comparing three BVH variants (naive CPU BVH, LBVH on CPU, LBVH on GPU) across four standard test models: Bunny (5K tris), Armadillo (213K), Dragon (871K), and Lucy (28M).

#### GPU Wins, But Only Once There's Enough Work to Hide the Overhead

The construction time numbers tell a pretty clean story once you look at where the crossover happens. For the Bunny (5K triangles), GPU LBVH is actually the *slowest* option - 94.73ms versus 2.62ms for CPU LBVH - because OpenCL initialization and kernel launch overhead completely dominates at that scale. There just isn't enough work to amortize the cost of spinning up the GPU pipeline.

But that flips hard as complexity increases. By the Dragon (871K triangles), GPU LBVH construction takes 181.34ms versus 448.30ms for CPU LBVH - already ahead. And for Lucy (28 million triangles), it's 3,008.95ms versus 13,988.55ms on CPU: a 4.65x speedup, and a full order of magnitude faster than the naive CPU BVH's 30.9 *seconds*. Breaking down the GPU-only kernel time confirms the radix sort is the expensive part of the pipeline - for Lucy it accounts for 141ms out of roughly 207ms of total kernel time, which lines up with what Karras reports in his own writeup.

The tree quality tradeoff is real but small. LBVH trees need somewhat more bounding-box tests per ray than the naive median-split BVH (48.56 vs. 31.64 average for Lucy), since Morton-order locality doesn't perfectly optimize traversal the way an explicit split heuristic can. But primitive intersection counts stay nearly identical across all three methods, and - reassuringly - CPU LBVH and GPU LBVH produce *exactly* the same traversal statistics, since they're the same algorithm just running on different hardware. That was a good sanity check that the GPU implementation was actually correct and not just fast.

## Final Thoughts

Turning BVH construction into a sorting problem trades a small amount of tree quality for an enormous amount of parallelism - and on the GPU, that trade only starts paying off once there's enough geometry to amortize the fixed overhead of getting the GPU involved in the first place. Below a few hundred thousand primitives, don't bother; above that, it's not close. This also reframes construction cost entirely: for dynamic, per-frame-rebuilt scenes, LBVH-on-GPU isn't just "an option," it's basically the only approach that keeps up.

Morton code computation, radix sort, hierarchy construction, and bounding-box propagation were all implemented from scratch as OpenCL kernels. The supplementary GPU path tracer used purely to render the benchmark images leaned heavily on AI assistance, since it wasn't the focus of the project - full disclosure is in the repo README.
